chapterSources.author: Antonio Damasio
chapterSources.title: Descartes' Error
chapterSources.note: The somatic marker hypothesis: bodily feeling is first-order, deliberation is second-order. Without somatic markers, patients can reason but cannot decide.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Before Thought, There Is Will

chapterSources.author: Antonio Damasio
chapterSources.title: The Feeling of What Happens
chapterSources.note: Consciousness itself as the feeling of what happens; the organism's orientation precedes any conceptual self.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Before Thought, There Is Will

chapterSources.author: Schopenhauer
chapterSources.title: The World as Will and Representation
chapterSources.note: Will as the thing-in-itself; intellect subordinate to drive. The most direct philosophical ancestor of volo ergo sum.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Before Thought, There Is Will

chapterSources.author: Spinoza
chapterSources.title: Ethics, Part III
chapterSources.note: Conatus: we judge something good because we strive for it, not the other way around. Desire is ontologically prior to evaluation.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Before Thought, There Is Will

chapterSources.author: Varela, Thompson & Rosch
chapterSources.title: The Embodied Mind
chapterSources.note: Enactivism: orientation and wanting are the substrate of cognition, not an add-on to it.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Before Thought, There Is Will

chapterSources.author: Lisa Feldman Barrett
chapterSources.title: How Emotions Are Made
chapterSources.note: The brain as an allostatic predictor: wanting and orienting are its baseline mode, not reactions to the world.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Before Thought, There Is Will

chapterSources.author: Anil Seth
chapterSources.title: Being You
chapterSources.note: Consciousness as controlled hallucination. Wanting has a first-person character that neuroscience is only beginning to model from the inside.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Before Thought, There Is Will

chapterSources.author: Kevin Mitchell
chapterSources.title: Free Agents
chapterSources.note: How nervous systems evolved to generate genuine agency rather than mere responsiveness: the biological story of why want precedes thought.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Before Thought, There Is Will

chapterSources.author: Ernest Becker
chapterSources.title: The Denial of Death
chapterSources.note: Death-awareness is the specific disruption that elevates animal want into human will. Knowing we will die, we cannot simply follow instinct but must choose what to lean toward, and that gap is where the book lives.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Before Thought, There Is Will

chapterSources.author: William James
chapterSources.title: A Pluralistic Universe
chapterSources.note: Reality is irreducibly multiple; divergence between streams of experience is structural, not accidental.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Will Creates Difference, Which Creates Problems

chapterSources.author: Gilbert Simondon
chapterSources.title: Individuation in Light of Notions of Form and Information
chapterSources.note: The most rigorous account of individuation as process: disparation (incompatible tensions) is the engine of selfhood.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Will Creates Difference, Which Creates Problems

chapterSources.author: Hegel
chapterSources.title: Phenomenology of Spirit
chapterSources.note: Individuation through encounter with difference; determinate negation means every contradiction resolves into something new rather than nothing.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Will Creates Difference, Which Creates Problems

chapterSources.author: W. Brian Arthur
chapterSources.title: Increasing Returns and Path Dependence in the Economy
chapterSources.note: Small early differences lock in large outcomes through positive feedback: path dependence as a general consequence of divergent wanting.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Will Creates Difference, Which Creates Problems

chapterSources.author: Stuart Kauffman
chapterSources.title: At Home in the Universe
chapterSources.note: Stable structures emerge from the collision of many divergent elements without any top-down design. Order for free.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Will Creates Difference, Which Creates Problems

chapterSources.author: Heraclitus
chapterSources.title: Fragments
chapterSources.note: All things come into being by conflict of opposites. The oldest argument that difference and conflict are generative rather than merely destructive.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Will Creates Difference, Which Creates Problems

chapterSources.author: Martin Buber
chapterSources.title: I and Thou
chapterSources.note: Love as mutual orientation enacted between beings: not a feeling one has but a mode of relating one enacts together.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Love, Growth, and Meaning (Which Are, It Turns Out, Related)

chapterSources.author: Iris Murdoch
chapterSources.title: The Sovereignty of Good
chapterSources.note: Love as just and loving attention, the method of all virtues; attention leads to growth leads to meaning.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Love, Growth, and Meaning (Which Are, It Turns Out, Related)

chapterSources.author: Harry Frankfurt
chapterSources.title: The Importance of What We Care About
chapterSources.note: Caring integrates the self across time; love is the paradigm case of what it means to be a person with a volitional essence.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Love, Growth, and Meaning (Which Are, It Turns Out, Related)

chapterSources.author: Viktor Frankl
chapterSources.title: Man's Search for Meaning
chapterSources.note: Will to meaning as the primary motivational force; emptiness is the existential vacuum produced by misaligned willing.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Love, Growth, and Meaning (Which Are, It Turns Out, Related)

chapterSources.author: Aristotle
chapterSources.title: Nicomachean Ethics, Books VIII-IX
chapterSources.note: Philia, eudaimonia, and growth through shared virtuous activity: love, meaning, and growth unified in one account from the start.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Love, Growth, and Meaning (Which Are, It Turns Out, Related)

chapterSources.author: Deci & Ryan
chapterSources.title: Self-Determination Theory
chapterSources.note: Empirical: autonomy, competence, and relatedness are universal psychological needs; growth is indexed to their alignment.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Love, Growth, and Meaning (Which Are, It Turns Out, Related)

chapterSources.author: Martha Nussbaum
chapterSources.title: Upheavals of Thought
chapterSources.note: Emotions as intelligent responses to value: love as a form of practical reasoning that constitutes rather than merely expresses the self.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Love, Growth, and Meaning (Which Are, It Turns Out, Related)

chapterSources.author: Simone de Beauvoir
chapterSources.title: The Ethics of Ambiguity
chapterSources.note: Freedom requires others to be free. Love and growth are not private achievements but ethical stakes in a shared world.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Love, Growth, and Meaning (Which Are, It Turns Out, Related)

chapterSources.author: Ernest Becker
chapterSources.title: The Denial of Death
chapterSources.note: Immortality projects as the primary human meaning-making strategy: love, heroism, and creative work as attempts to transcend biological finitude; meaning is not just durable wanting but wanting pressed against the fact of death.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Love, Growth, and Meaning (Which Are, It Turns Out, Related)

chapterSources.author: Thomas Nagel
chapterSources.title: The View from Nowhere
chapterSources.note: Objectivity is a hard-won partial achievement, not a god's-eye view, and the attempt to approximate it is what science is.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: From Subjectivity to Something That Will Have to Do

chapterSources.author: Hannah Arendt
chapterSources.title: The Human Condition
chapterSources.note: Plurality: reality is guaranteed not by a common nature but by many distinct people being concerned with the same object.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: From Subjectivity to Something That Will Have to Do

chapterSources.author: Donald Davidson
chapterSources.title: Subjective, Intersubjective, Objective
chapterSources.note: Triangulation: objective truth requires two agents responding to shared causes in the world. Objectivity emerges from intersubjectivity.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: From Subjectivity to Something That Will Have to Do

chapterSources.author: Wilfrid Sellars
chapterSources.title: Empiricism and the Philosophy of Mind
chapterSources.note: The myth of the given: perception is already conceptually structured. Nothing in experience is incorrigibly given as a foundation.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: From Subjectivity to Something That Will Have to Do

chapterSources.author: John Searle
chapterSources.title: The Construction of Social Reality
chapterSources.note: Institutional facts via collective intentionality. Objectivity is constructed but not arbitrary; it requires ongoing collective recognition.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: From Subjectivity to Something That Will Have to Do

chapterSources.author: Michael Tomasello
chapterSources.title: The Cultural Origins of Human Cognition
chapterSources.note: Empirical: objectivity is developmentally downstream of shared intentionality, not prior to it.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: From Subjectivity to Something That Will Have to Do

chapterSources.author: George Spencer-Brown
chapterSources.title: Laws of Form
chapterSources.note: The act of drawing a distinction is the primordial act. We cannot make an indication without drawing a distinction first.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The First Blade: The Catastrophic Invention of Edges

chapterSources.author: Maturana & Varela
chapterSources.title: Autopoiesis and Cognition
chapterSources.note: Living systems produce the very boundary that defines them: identity and edge are co-constituted, not pre-given.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The First Blade: The Catastrophic Invention of Edges

chapterSources.author: Merleau-Ponty
chapterSources.title: Phenomenology of Perception
chapterSources.note: The body schema enacts a pre-reflective self/not-self boundary; phantom limb cases show the cut is operational, not anatomical.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The First Blade: The Catastrophic Invention of Edges

chapterSources.author: Jakob von Uexkull
chapterSources.title: A Foray Into the Worlds of Animals and Humans
chapterSources.note: Each organism's Umwelt is a distinct informational carving of reality; the cut is species-specific and task-specific.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The First Blade: The Catastrophic Invention of Edges

chapterSources.author: Polly Matzinger
chapterSources.title: The Danger Model: A Renewed Sense of Self
chapterSources.note: Paradigm-shifting immunology: the immune boundary responds to damage signals, not mere foreignness. The cut is enacted, not fixed.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The First Blade: The Catastrophic Invention of Edges

chapterSources.author: Aristotle
chapterSources.title: Categories
chapterSources.note: The first systematic account of what kinds of things there are: the philosophical origin of the edge-drawing project.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The First Blade: The Catastrophic Invention of Edges

chapterSources.author: Achille Varzi
chapterSources.title: Parts and Places
chapterSources.note: When do boundaries exist, and for whom? Fiat versus bona fide boundaries: the metaphysical backbone of what the chapter describes as catastrophic.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The First Blade: The Catastrophic Invention of Edges

chapterSources.author: Alfred Korzybski
chapterSources.title: Science and Sanity
chapterSources.note: Source of the canonical slogan. At minimum two representational layers separate us from reality; pathology follows when people act as if there are none.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Second Blade: The Map and the Territory (One of Which Is Wrong)

chapterSources.author: Andy Clark
chapterSources.title: Surfing Uncertainty
chapterSources.note: The brain as a prediction machine. Perception is controlled hallucination constrained by prediction error, not a passive mirror.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Second Blade: The Map and the Territory (One of Which Is Wrong)

chapterSources.author: Karl Friston
chapterSources.title: The Free-Energy Principle: A Unified Brain Theory?
chapterSources.note: Variational free energy: the brain minimises surprise by either updating its model or acting to make its predictions true.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Second Blade: The Map and the Territory (One of Which Is Wrong)

chapterSources.author: Gregory Bateson
chapterSources.title: Steps to an Ecology of Mind
chapterSources.note: Information is a difference that makes a difference. Maps transduce rather than copy, and that is why they can be wrong.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Second Blade: The Map and the Territory (One of Which Is Wrong)

chapterSources.author: Karl Popper
chapterSources.title: Conjectures and Refutations
chapterSources.note: Falsificationism: the gap between map and territory is not a tragedy but the engine of learning. Error is structural.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Second Blade: The Map and the Territory (One of Which Is Wrong)

chapterSources.author: Thomas Kuhn
chapterSources.title: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
chapterSources.note: Paradigms are maps scaled to whole communities. Paradigm shifts are forced corrections when anomalies overwhelm the existing model.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Second Blade: The Map and the Territory (One of Which Is Wrong)

chapterSources.author: C.S. Peirce
chapterSources.title: Collected Papers (signs and inquiry)
chapterSources.note: The most rigorous theory of how signs work: fallibilism as the epistemological consequence of the map/territory gap.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Second Blade: The Map and the Territory (One of Which Is Wrong)

chapterSources.author: Nelson Goodman
chapterSources.title: Ways of Worldmaking
chapterSources.note: Multiple worlds made by multiple maps, under rigorous constraints: radical constructive pluralism without collapsing into relativism.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Second Blade: The Map and the Territory (One of Which Is Wrong)

chapterSources.author: Douglas Hofstadter
chapterSources.title: Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid
chapterSources.note: The original long argument that self-reference through a physical substrate is the signature of mind, traced through formal systems, music, and art.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Second Blade: The Map and the Territory (One of Which Is Wrong)

chapterSources.author: Douglas Hofstadter
chapterSources.title: I Am a Strange Loop
chapterSources.note: A tighter restatement: the self is not a thing but a loop, a low-resolution model of the pattern-maker running on the matter that carries it.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Second Blade: The Map and the Territory (One of Which Is Wrong)

chapterSources.author: Antonio Damasio
chapterSources.title: Descartes' Error
chapterSources.note: Somatic markers as rapid pre-cognitive valence signals: patients who lose them retain logic but cannot decide.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Third Blade: Good, Bad, and the Trouble with Both

chapterSources.author: Jaak Panksepp
chapterSources.title: Affective Neuroscience
chapterSources.note: Seven primary emotional command systems in subcortical structures homologous across all mammals. Valence comes first, cortex follows.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Third Blade: Good, Bad, and the Trouble with Both

chapterSources.author: Kent Berridge
chapterSources.title: Dissecting Components of Reward: Liking, Wanting, and Learning
chapterSources.note: Wanting (dopamine) and liking (opioid systems) are dissociable. Good is not one blade but at minimum two.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Third Blade: Good, Bad, and the Trouble with Both

chapterSources.author: Evan Thompson
chapterSources.title: Mind in Life
chapterSources.note: Bacterial chemotaxis as proto-valuation: sense-making is continuous from the simplest life up through human consciousness.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Third Blade: Good, Bad, and the Trouble with Both

chapterSources.author: Joseph LeDoux
chapterSources.title: The Emotional Brain
chapterSources.note: The amygdala's low road: the body is assigned a valence before consciousness catches up. Navigation precedes reflection.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Third Blade: Good, Bad, and the Trouble with Both

chapterSources.author: Jesse Prinz
chapterSources.title: Gut Reactions
chapterSources.note: Embodied appraisals: emotions are perceptions of bodily states that simultaneously constitute evaluations of what matters.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Third Blade: Good, Bad, and the Trouble with Both

chapterSources.author: Nietzsche
chapterSources.title: On the Genealogy of Morality
chapterSources.note: Values have histories and serve interests; tracing the blade of good/bad back to who wielded it and why it was sharpened that way.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Third Blade: Good, Bad, and the Trouble with Both

chapterSources.author: Max Scheler
chapterSources.title: Formalism in Ethics and Non-Formal Ethics of Values
chapterSources.note: Values are felt and perceived before they are judged: a phenomenology of the value-sensing apparatus that precedes any explicit ethics.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Third Blade: Good, Bad, and the Trouble with Both

chapterSources.author: Philippa Foot
chapterSources.title: Natural Goodness
chapterSources.note: Goodness for a living thing is not a projection onto neutral matter but a biological reality: the third blade has a natural history.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Third Blade: Good, Bad, and the Trouble with Both

chapterSources.author: Alasdair MacIntyre
chapterSources.title: After Virtue
chapterSources.note: We lost the context (tradition, telos) that made value-talk coherent. The trouble with good and bad is partly a historical wound.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Third Blade: Good, Bad, and the Trouble with Both

chapterSources.author: Claude Levi-Strauss
chapterSources.title: Structural Anthropology
chapterSources.note: The human mind universally operates by binary opposition; myths exist to manage irresolvable tensions rather than to resolve them.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Foundational Dualities (There Are More Than You'd Like)

chapterSources.author: Mark Johnson
chapterSources.title: The Body in the Mind
chapterSources.note: Image schemas (CONTAINMENT, FORCE, VERTICALITY) show that binary structure has a bodily ground floor. It comes from having a body.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Foundational Dualities (There Are More Than You'd Like)

chapterSources.author: Hegel
chapterSources.title: Science of Logic
chapterSources.note: Each concept contains its own negation; oppositions are generative engines, not stable resting points.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Foundational Dualities (There Are More Than You'd Like)

chapterSources.author: Gregory Bateson
chapterSources.title: Toward a Theory of Schizophrenia
chapterSources.note: Double bind: the pathology of a duality that cannot be held as a duality, i.e. what happens when the two poles must both be true.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Foundational Dualities (There Are More Than You'd Like)

chapterSources.author: Carl Jung
chapterSources.title: Aion
chapterSources.note: Shadow as structural: the ego maintains coherence by suppressing its opposite into the unconscious, not by eliminating it.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Foundational Dualities (There Are More Than You'd Like)

chapterSources.author: Xinyan Jiang
chapterSources.title: Chinese Dialectical Thinking: The Yin Yang Model
chapterSources.note: Key asymmetry: Western dialectics tends toward supersession; yin-yang holds the poles as mutually constitutive and containing each other.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Foundational Dualities (There Are More Than You'd Like)

chapterSources.author: Robert M. Pirsig
chapterSources.title: Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance
chapterSources.note: Quality is the prior unity from which subject and object are carved; every duality is a cut in something that was whole first.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Foundational Dualities (There Are More Than You'd Like)

chapterSources.author: John Searle
chapterSources.title: The Construction of Social Reality
chapterSources.note: X counts as Y in context C: the mechanism by which collective declarations create institutional things with genuine causal power.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Thingification, or How Fog Becomes a Tax Code

chapterSources.author: Alfred North Whitehead
chapterSources.title: Science and the Modern World
chapterSources.note: The fallacy of misplaced concreteness: mistaking an abstraction for the concrete reality from which it was abstracted.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Thingification, or How Fog Becomes a Tax Code

chapterSources.author: Gyorgy Lukacs
chapterSources.title: History and Class Consciousness
chapterSources.note: Reification (Verdinglichung): dynamic human relations harden into thing-like objects and forget they were ever relations.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Thingification, or How Fog Becomes a Tax Code

chapterSources.author: Eleanor Rosch
chapterSources.title: Principles of Categorization
chapterSources.note: Empirical: categories are prototype-structured with graded membership, not defined by necessary and sufficient conditions.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Thingification, or How Fog Becomes a Tax Code

chapterSources.author: Hofstadter & Sander
chapterSources.title: Surfaces and Essences
chapterSources.note: Categories as frozen analogies: fog becomes tax code via the crystallisation of once-active comparisons into habitual classifications.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Thingification, or How Fog Becomes a Tax Code

chapterSources.author: Wittgenstein
chapterSources.title: Philosophical Investigations
chapterSources.note: Family resemblance: no single property is shared by all members of a natural category, a philosophical result Rosch later confirmed empirically.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Thingification, or How Fog Becomes a Tax Code

chapterSources.author: Berger & Luckmann
chapterSources.title: The Social Construction of Reality
chapterSources.note: The foundational sociology of how shared thingifications become taken-for-granted reality: habitualisation, institutionalisation, legitimation.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Thingification, or How Fog Becomes a Tax Code

chapterSources.author: Bowker & Star
chapterSources.title: Sorting Things Out
chapterSources.note: Classification systems as moral and political acts. The lived cost of being placed in the wrong category is distributed unequally.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Thingification, or How Fog Becomes a Tax Code

chapterSources.author: James C. Scott
chapterSources.title: Seeing Like a State
chapterSources.note: State simplification of complex reality produces both power and catastrophic failure. Legibility is a blade that cuts back.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Thingification, or How Fog Becomes a Tax Code

chapterSources.author: David Graeber
chapterSources.title: The Utopia of Rules
chapterSources.note: Bureaucracy as crystallised thingification: how fog becomes not just a tax code but a structural instrument of control.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Thingification, or How Fog Becomes a Tax Code

chapterSources.author: Norbert Wiener
chapterSources.title: Cybernetics
chapterSources.note: Information is information, not matter or energy. The irreducibility of the informational domain announced at the founding of cybernetics.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Information / Physical Duality (Both Are Real, Which Is Inconvenient)

chapterSources.author: Claude Shannon
chapterSources.title: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
chapterSources.note: Information defined structurally and independently of physical substrate or semantic content: the same information can live in electrons, neurons, or ink.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Information / Physical Duality (Both Are Real, Which Is Inconvenient)

chapterSources.author: Gregory Bateson
chapterSources.title: Form, Substance and Difference
chapterSources.note: A difference that makes a difference. Organism-relative information: a difference only counts for a system it matters to.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Information / Physical Duality (Both Are Real, Which Is Inconvenient)

chapterSources.author: John Archibald Wheeler
chapterSources.title: Information, Physics, Quantum: The Search for Links
chapterSources.note: It from Bit: every physical entity derives its existence from answers to yes-or-no questions. The most radical statement of informational primacy.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Information / Physical Duality (Both Are Real, Which Is Inconvenient)

chapterSources.author: Terrence Deacon
chapterSources.title: Incomplete Nature
chapterSources.note: The causal power of information comes from constraints (absences), not from physical properties. The most philosophically rigorous recent argument.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Information / Physical Duality (Both Are Real, Which Is Inconvenient)

chapterSources.author: Luciano Floridi
chapterSources.title: The Philosophy of Information
chapterSources.note: Informational structural realism: a bridge from Shannon's syntax to meaningful semantic information as a full research programme.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Information / Physical Duality (Both Are Real, Which Is Inconvenient)

chapterSources.author: Howard Pattee & Joanna Raczaszek-Leonardi
chapterSources.title: Laws, Language and Life
chapterSources.note: The epistemic cut: where physical substrate and symbolic control separate. The most precise technical account of how information and matter interface.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Information / Physical Duality (Both Are Real, Which Is Inconvenient)

chapterSources.author: Robert Rosen
chapterSources.title: Life Itself
chapterSources.note: Life as anticipatory system: the informational loop that distinguishes living from non-living matter runs on models of the future, not just responses to the past.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Information / Physical Duality (Both Are Real, Which Is Inconvenient)

chapterSources.author: Michel Foucault
chapterSources.title: The Order of Things
chapterSources.note: The episteme as a cut through possible thought; within it, certain questions become literally unaskable. His opening meditation on Borges' Chinese encyclopedia is directly on point.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Cost of the Blade

chapterSources.author: Simone de Beauvoir
chapterSources.title: The Second Sex
chapterSources.note: One is not born, but becomes, a woman. The cost of a category is borne by those assigned to it.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Cost of the Blade

chapterSources.author: Edward Said
chapterSources.title: Orientalism
chapterSources.note: Categorical systems as exercises of power: the cut that produces knowledge simultaneously forgets that it was made.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Cost of the Blade

chapterSources.author: George Lakoff
chapterSources.title: Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things
chapterSources.note: Every categorical system reveals the categoriser's embodied, cultural situation. Categories are not windows onto the world but portraits of the cutter.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Cost of the Blade

chapterSources.author: Paul Ricoeur
chapterSources.title: The Rule of Metaphor
chapterSources.note: Living metaphors die into categories: the productive cut first shocks, then becomes invisible, then becomes a prison.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Cost of the Blade

chapterSources.author: Richard Rorty
chapterSources.title: Contingency, Irony, and Solidarity
chapterSources.note: All categories are final vocabularies; forgetting their contingency is what produces fanaticism.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Cost of the Blade

chapterSources.author: Eugene Wigner
chapterSources.title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences
chapterSources.note: The essay that named the puzzle: why does abstract math fit physical law so astonishingly well? The question this chapter gently deflates.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Knowledge, or the Shape of the Information Realm

chapterSources.author: Kurt Gödel
chapterSources.title: On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems
chapterSources.note: The original incompleteness paper. Read it to see how narrow the claim actually is before anyone dresses it up.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Knowledge, or the Shape of the Information Realm

chapterSources.author: Ernest Nagel & James R. Newman
chapterSources.title: Gödel's Proof
chapterSources.note: The short accessible exposition that gets the argument across without importing mysticism on the way.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Knowledge, or the Shape of the Information Realm

chapterSources.author: Torkel Franzén
chapterSources.title: Gödel's Theorem: An Incomplete Guide to Its Use and Abuse
chapterSources.note: The definitive hygiene manual: a patient catalogue of what the theorem does and does not license anyone to say.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Knowledge, or the Shape of the Information Realm

chapterSources.author: Thomas Kuhn
chapterSources.title: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
chapterSources.note: Science as a plural practice with paradigms, not a single voice of Reason. Useful for seeing disciplines as communities with instruments.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Knowledge, or the Shape of the Information Realm

chapterSources.author: C.P. Snow
chapterSources.title: The Two Cultures
chapterSources.note: The classic diagnosis of the rift between scientific and humanistic knowledge, and why pretending one is the only game is expensive.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Knowledge, or the Shape of the Information Realm

chapterSources.author: Imre Lakatos
chapterSources.title: Proofs and Refutations
chapterSources.note: Mathematics reconstructed as a living argumentative practice rather than a sealed deductive monument.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Knowledge, or the Shape of the Information Realm

chapterSources.author: Georges Ifrah
chapterSources.title: The Universal History of Numbers
chapterSources.note: How counting systems actually grew across cultures, with the tallies, tokens, and notations that show unit-making preceding arithmetic.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Knowledge, or the Shape of the Information Realm

chapterSources.author: Naomi Oreskes & Erik Conway
chapterSources.title: Merchants of Doubt
chapterSources.note: A case study in disciplines going bad on purpose: credentialed smoke produced to stall policy for a generation.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Knowledge, or the Shape of the Information Realm

chapterSources.author: Gregory Bateson
chapterSources.title: Steps to an Ecology of Mind
chapterSources.note: Bateson's learning levels (Learning I, II, III) anticipate the cycle structure: each level operates on a different logical type.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Three Cycles

chapterSources.author: Ken Wilber
chapterSources.title: Integral Psychology
chapterSources.note: Developmental stages that include pre-personal, personal, and trans-personal modes — a related but distinct gradient.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Three Cycles

chapterSources.author: Iain McGilchrist
chapterSources.title: The Master and His Emissary
chapterSources.note: The left hemisphere's focused, analytical grasp vs. the right hemisphere's open, contextual attention maps loosely onto Learning vs. Becoming.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Three Cycles

chapterSources.author: Ian Hacking
chapterSources.title: Representing and Intervening
chapterSources.note: Measurement involves intervening, not just representing. The instrument is already a model, already a theory about what matters.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Learning: Measure, Model, Manipulate

chapterSources.author: Karl Popper
chapterSources.title: The Logic of Scientific Discovery
chapterSources.note: Falsifiability as the demarcation criterion — a model is scientific if it specifies what would prove it wrong.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Learning: Measure, Model, Manipulate

chapterSources.author: Judea Pearl
chapterSources.title: Causality
chapterSources.note: The formal framework for distinguishing correlation from causation. Manipulation (intervention) is how we learn causal structure.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Learning: Measure, Model, Manipulate

chapterSources.author: David Marr
chapterSources.title: Vision
chapterSources.note: Three levels of analysis: computational, algorithmic, implementational. A model can be correct at one level and wrong at another.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Learning: Measure, Model, Manipulate

chapterSources.author: James C. Scott
chapterSources.title: Seeing Like a State
chapterSources.note: The difference between scientific forestry (Learning-style mapping) and practical navigation (Creating-style mapping) — metis vs. techne.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Creating: Map, Move, Make

chapterSources.author: Tim Ingold
chapterSources.title: The Perception of the Environment
chapterSources.note: Wayfinding as skilled practice: you don't follow a map, you navigate a world. Movement creates knowledge.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Creating: Map, Move, Make

chapterSources.author: Richard Sennett
chapterSources.title: The Craftsman
chapterSources.note: Making as a mode of understanding. The hand teaches the head. Skill develops through doing, not just knowing.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Creating: Map, Move, Make

chapterSources.author: Matthew Crawford
chapterSources.title: Shop Class as Soulcraft
chapterSources.note: The cognitive demands of manual work. Making is thinking with materials.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Creating: Map, Move, Make

chapterSources.author: Abraham Maslow
chapterSources.title: Religions, Values, and Peak Experiences
chapterSources.note: Peak experiences as moments of Marvel — self-validating, non-instrumental awareness.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Becoming: Marvel, Meander, Manifest

chapterSources.author: Rebecca Solnit
chapterSources.title: A Field Guide to Getting Lost
chapterSources.note: The generative capacity of wandering and uncertainty. Not knowing where you're going as a condition of discovery.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Becoming: Marvel, Meander, Manifest

chapterSources.author: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi
chapterSources.title: Flow
chapterSources.note: Flow states as a bridge — Creating skill meeting something like Becoming surrender.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Becoming: Marvel, Meander, Manifest

chapterSources.author: Martin Buber
chapterSources.title: I and Thou
chapterSources.note: The distinction between I-It (Learning and Creating) and I-Thou (Becoming). Encounter vs. experience.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Becoming: Marvel, Meander, Manifest

chapterSources.author: Robert Kegan
chapterSources.title: In Over Our Heads
chapterSources.note: Developmental orders of consciousness — a framework for thinking about how later stages incorporate earlier ones.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Cycles in Relation

chapterSources.author: Terri O'Fallon
chapterSources.title: StAGES Model
chapterSources.note: Empirical research on developmental stages including post-conventional, integrative structures.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Cycles in Relation

chapterSources.author: Clare Graves
chapterSources.title: Levels of Existence
chapterSources.note: The original research behind Spiral Dynamics — emergent, cyclical developmental stages.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Cycles in Relation

chapterSources.author: David Kolb
chapterSources.title: Experiential Learning
chapterSources.note: Four-stage cycle (Experience to Reflection to Conceptualisation to Experimentation): MMM at pedagogical scale, drawing on Dewey, Piaget, and Lewin.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: MMM as the Lived Experience of Growth

chapterSources.author: Argyris & Schon
chapterSources.title: Organizational Learning
chapterSources.note: Single-loop vs double-loop learning: optimising within a model vs replacing the model itself. Organizations systematically resist the second.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: MMM as the Lived Experience of Growth

chapterSources.author: John Boyd
chapterSources.title: Destruction and Creation
chapterSources.note: OODA loop: Orient (the Model step) is where the real competitive advantage lives; speed through the loop beats better sensors or stronger action.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: MMM as the Lived Experience of Growth

chapterSources.author: Gregory Bateson
chapterSources.title: Steps to an Ecology of Mind
chapterSources.note: Learning I/II/III hierarchy: Learning III is radical recontextualization, rare, difficult, and often accompanied by the dissolution of self.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: MMM as the Lived Experience of Growth

chapterSources.author: Jean Piaget
chapterSources.title: The Psychology of Intelligence
chapterSources.note: Assimilation and accommodation: the organism fits experience to existing schema, or changes the schema to fit. Equilibration drives development.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: MMM as the Lived Experience of Growth

chapterSources.author: Lev Vygotsky
chapterSources.title: Thought and Language
chapterSources.note: Zone of proximal development: the MMM loop is most generative not at mastered skills or impossible tasks but at the edge of current competence.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: MMM as the Lived Experience of Growth

chapterSources.author: Emmanuel Dupoux, Yann LeCun & Jitendra Malik
chapterSources.title: Why AI systems don't learn and what to do about it: Lessons on autonomous learning from cognitive science
chapterSources.note: Proposes a three-system architecture for autonomous intelligence: System A (observation learning), System B (active-behavior learning), and System M (meta-control that switches between them). A structural echo of Measure, Model, Manifest: the same three-layer shape reappearing from a different discipline. Independent convergence, not influence.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: MMM as the Lived Experience of Growth

chapterSources.author: Ian Hacking
chapterSources.title: The Social Construction of What?
chapterSources.note: Looping effects of human kinds: classifying people changes the people classified, which changes the classification. The mechanism by which informational labels become physical territory.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Applied Knowledge, or How the Info Realm Folds Back

chapterSources.author: Bruno Latour
chapterSources.title: We Have Never Been Modern
chapterSources.note: Facts and artifacts are co-produced by networks of humans and things; the clean separation of knowledge from the world it describes was never tenable.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Applied Knowledge, or How the Info Realm Folds Back

chapterSources.author: Langdon Winner
chapterSources.title: Do Artifacts Have Politics?
chapterSources.note: A short, load-bearing essay: built things encode decisions, and those decisions keep making themselves long after the builders are gone.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Applied Knowledge, or How the Info Realm Folds Back

chapterSources.author: Ursula Franklin
chapterSources.title: The Real World of Technology
chapterSources.note: Holistic versus prescriptive technologies: once a prescriptive technology is adopted, it reshapes the practices around it until no other way remains visible.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Applied Knowledge, or How the Info Realm Folds Back

chapterSources.author: Edwin Hutchins
chapterSources.title: Cognition in the Wild
chapterSources.note: Cognition distributed across people and artifacts; the ship's navigation crew is a worked example of knowledge living partly outside any single head.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Applied Knowledge, or How the Info Realm Folds Back

chapterSources.author: Joseph Henrich
chapterSources.title: The Secret of Our Success
chapterSources.note: Cumulative cultural evolution: the capacity to inherit knowledge across generations is the human trick, and it runs through artifacts and institutions as much as through teaching.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Applied Knowledge, or How the Info Realm Folds Back

chapterSources.author: James C. Scott
chapterSources.title: Seeing Like a State
chapterSources.note: High-modernist projects fail when the imposed map overrides the local knowledge it displaces; a dark case study in world-changing by decree.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: How We Change the World

chapterSources.author: Jane Jacobs
chapterSources.title: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
chapterSources.note: Bottom-up world-changing at the scale of a city block: a defence of the slow, legible, corrigible Manifest against the spectacular one.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: How We Change the World

chapterSources.author: Elizabeth Eisenstein
chapterSources.title: The Printing Press as an Agent of Change
chapterSources.note: The cleanest historical case: one artifact quietly rearranges literacy, religion, science, and politics over centuries, with no single author in charge of the outcome.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: How We Change the World

chapterSources.author: Jared Diamond
chapterSources.title: Collapse
chapterSources.note: Societies that changed their worlds and then could not unchange them; a catalogue of civilisational loops that stalled because the feedback was read too late.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: How We Change the World

chapterSources.author: Ursula Franklin
chapterSources.title: The Real World of Technology
chapterSources.note: Distinguishes technologies that invite participation from those that prescribe it; a practical criterion for better and worse world-changing.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: How We Change the World

chapterSources.author: Vaclav Smil
chapterSources.title: Enriching the Earth
chapterSources.note: The Haber-Bosch process and the Green Revolution: billions fed, soils and atmospheres strained; a sober accounting of a world-changing intervention with real gifts and real costs.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: How We Change the World

chapterSources.author: Lynn Margulis
chapterSources.title: On the Origin of Mitosing Cells
chapterSources.note: Endosymbiosis as evolutionary MMM: a detected difference leads to a new cellular architecture leads to a radically new form of life, the eukaryote.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: MMM Across Life Itself (Including the Bits Without Brains)

chapterSources.author: Jablonka & Lamb
chapterSources.title: Evolution in Four Dimensions
chapterSources.note: Four inheritance systems (genetic, epigenetic, behavioural, symbolic) as stacked layers of MMM loop capacity added over evolutionary time.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: MMM Across Life Itself (Including the Bits Without Brains)

chapterSources.author: Terrence Deacon
chapterSources.title: Incomplete Nature
chapterSources.note: Teleodynamics: the condition under which something strives toward a goal and corrects deviations. The most rigorous account of how purposiveness emerges from matter.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: MMM Across Life Itself (Including the Bits Without Brains)

chapterSources.author: Stuart Kauffman
chapterSources.title: The Origins of Order
chapterSources.note: Self-organisation at the edge of chaos provides the ordered landscape that evolution searches. Natural selection alone cannot explain biological order.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: MMM Across Life Itself (Including the Bits Without Brains)

chapterSources.author: Daniel Dennett
chapterSources.title: Darwin's Dangerous Idea
chapterSources.note: Natural selection as universal acid: design can emerge from unintelligent cumulative processes. The philosophical framing for extending MMM to all life.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: MMM Across Life Itself (Including the Bits Without Brains)

chapterSources.author: W. Ross Ashby
chapterSources.title: An Introduction to Cybernetics
chapterSources.note: Law of requisite variety: a controller needs as much internal variety as the system it controls; the loop must match the complexity of what it regulates.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: MMM Across Life Itself (Including the Bits Without Brains)

chapterSources.author: Charles Darwin
chapterSources.title: On the Origin of Species
chapterSources.note: The foundational text: the MMM loop running without a brain, across geological time, through descent with modification and natural selection.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: MMM Across Life Itself (Including the Bits Without Brains)

chapterSources.author: Maynard Smith & Szathmary
chapterSources.title: The Major Transitions in Evolution
chapterSources.note: Each major transition is a new way of encoding and transmitting information: evolution as stacked MMM layers, each more compressed than the last.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: MMM Across Life Itself (Including the Bits Without Brains)

chapterSources.author: Odling-Smee, Laland & Feldman
chapterSources.title: Niche Construction
chapterSources.note: Organisms do not just adapt to environments, they build them; the Manifest step feeds back into Measure across generations.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: MMM Across Life Itself (Including the Bits Without Brains)

chapterSources.author: William James
chapterSources.title: The Varieties of Religious Experience
chapterSources.note: Rigorous empirical taxonomy of mystical states across traditions; pragmatic criterion: evaluate by fruits, not by origins.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: What the Mystics Were Tracking

chapterSources.author: Varela, Thompson & Rosch
chapterSources.title: The Embodied Mind
chapterSources.note: The formal bridge between Buddhist phenomenology and cognitive science via enaction: the traditions were doing applied first-person neuroscience.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: What the Mystics Were Tracking

chapterSources.author: Evan Thompson
chapterSources.title: Waking, Dreaming, Being
chapterSources.note: The self as a process across states of consciousness; contemplative traditions as systematic investigations of what models the self runs in different states.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: What the Mystics Were Tracking

chapterSources.author: Antonio Damasio
chapterSources.title: The Strange Order of Things
chapterSources.note: Spiritual practices as high-level homeostatic regulation: biological grounding without reduction; the mystics were tracking deviations from optimal states.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: What the Mystics Were Tracking

chapterSources.author: Simone Weil
chapterSources.title: Waiting for God
chapterSources.note: Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity: the Measure step of MMM described as a spiritual practice.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: What the Mystics Were Tracking

chapterSources.author: Richard Davidson et al.
chapterSources.title: Long-term meditators self-induce high-amplitude gamma synchrony
chapterSources.note: Empirical: expert meditators show the highest gamma amplitudes recorded in a non-pathological context. Attention training measurably changes the brain.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: What the Mystics Were Tracking

chapterSources.author: Zhuangzi (trans. Ziporyn)
chapterSources.title: Zhuangzi: The Essential Writings
chapterSources.note: Wu-wei and the useless tree: skillful action emerges from presence rather than calculation. The Daoist version of the MMM loop without a program.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: What the Mystics Were Tracking

chapterSources.author: Nagarjuna
chapterSources.title: Mulamadhyamakakarika
chapterSources.note: The most rigorous Buddhist argument that all phenomena lack inherent existence: even the blade has no handle of its own.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: What the Mystics Were Tracking

chapterSources.author: Bhagavad Gita
chapterSources.title: Bhagavad Gita
chapterSources.note: Action without attachment to fruits: the Manifest step freed from the anxiety of outcome. The battlefield as a practical ontology of action-under-clarity.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: What the Mystics Were Tracking

chapterSources.author: Meister Eckhart
chapterSources.title: Selected Sermons
chapterSources.note: Abgeschiedenheit (detachment) as the ground of the soul: attention as dissolution of the self-model that stands between you and reality.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: What the Mystics Were Tracking

chapterSources.author: Al-Ghazali
chapterSources.title: Deliverance from Error
chapterSources.note: The spiritual crisis of over-modeling: the mystic as someone who has noticed their map is a map. The philosophical route to trust in direct experience.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: What the Mystics Were Tracking

chapterSources.author: Ernest Becker
chapterSources.title: The Denial of Death
chapterSources.note: Terror management theory's deepest precursor: religion and mystical practice as culturally sanctioned systems for metabolising death anxiety. What the mystics were tracking, at one level, is the problem Becker names.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: What the Mystics Were Tracking

chapterSources.author: Daniel Kahneman
chapterSources.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
chapterSources.note: System 1 as the background model-layer: the chapter's project is making automatic, invisible models legible to the slower, deliberate mind.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: How to Live Better, Given Everything

chapterSources.author: Hayes, Strosahl & Wilson
chapterSources.title: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy
chapterSources.note: Six ACT processes map cleanly onto Measure/Model/Manifest; psychological flexibility is the operational version of living the MMM loop. Over 1,200 RCTs.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: How to Live Better, Given Everything

chapterSources.author: Viktor Frankl
chapterSources.title: Man's Search for Meaning
chapterSources.note: Logotherapy: meaning as the primary motivational force; the existential vacuum (emptiness) is the pathology the MMM framework is designed to address.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: How to Live Better, Given Everything

chapterSources.author: Epictetus
chapterSources.title: Enchiridion
chapterSources.note: The dichotomy of control: what lies in our judgments and what does not. Prohairesis (the rational choice-faculty) is the Model-revision faculty applied to emotional response.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: How to Live Better, Given Everything

chapterSources.author: Irvin Yalom
chapterSources.title: Existential Psychotherapy
chapterSources.note: Four ultimate concerns (death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness): defective background models around each generate specific, recognisable pathologies.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: How to Live Better, Given Everything

chapterSources.author: Carl Rogers
chapterSources.title: The Necessary and Sufficient Conditions of Therapeutic Personality Change
chapterSources.note: Unconditional positive regard creates a relational scaffold in which the client's Measure step can function without distortion; trust enables accurate sensing.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: How to Live Better, Given Everything

chapterSources.author: Santideva
chapterSources.title: Bodhicaryavatara (The Way of the Bodhisattva)
chapterSources.note: Patient attention to others' suffering as the foundation of how to live; the capability approach has roots here, before economics formalised it.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: How to Live Better, Given Everything

chapterSources.author: Martha Nussbaum
chapterSources.title: The Fragility of Goodness
chapterSources.note: Vulnerability as a condition for flourishing, not a defect: what it means to live well under genuine uncertainty rather than in spite of it.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: How to Live Better, Given Everything

chapterSources.author: Amartya Sen
chapterSources.title: Development as Freedom
chapterSources.note: Capabilities rather than utility: what matters is what people are able to do and be. The framework applied at civilisational scale.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: How to Live Better, Given Everything

chapterSources.author: Donna Haraway
chapterSources.title: Situated Knowledges
chapterSources.note: The god trick of the view from nowhere: embodied objectivity via acknowledged partiality is not relativism but the only route to genuine connection.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Most Objective We Can Be (Which Is, Admittedly, Not Very)

chapterSources.author: Thomas Nagel
chapterSources.title: The View from Nowhere
chapterSources.note: Objectivity as an ideal that can never be fully achieved. Nagel and Haraway are not opposites but two sides of the same honest position.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Most Objective We Can Be (Which Is, Admittedly, Not Very)

chapterSources.author: Heather Douglas
chapterSources.title: Science, Policy, and the Value-Free Ideal
chapterSources.note: Values play a legitimate indirect role in scientific reasoning; her seven senses of objectivity provide the most useful taxonomy for the chapter's argument.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Most Objective We Can Be (Which Is, Admittedly, Not Very)

chapterSources.author: Helen Longino
chapterSources.title: Science as Social Knowledge
chapterSources.note: Objectivity is a property of communities of inquiry, not individual scientists. Disciplined approximation requires the right social infrastructure.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Most Objective We Can Be (Which Is, Admittedly, Not Very)

chapterSources.author: Charles Sanders Peirce
chapterSources.title: The Fixation of Belief
chapterSources.note: Objectivity as a disposition: the commitment to following evidence against one's own prior beliefs, and the community that makes this stable over time.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Most Objective We Can Be (Which Is, Admittedly, Not Very)

chapterSources.author: Open Science Collaboration
chapterSources.title: Estimating the Reproducibility of Psychological Science
chapterSources.note: The replication crisis is not an argument for relativism. It is the sharpest empirical demonstration that objectivity requires tracking consequences.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Most Objective We Can Be (Which Is, Admittedly, Not Very)

chapterSources.author: William James
chapterSources.title: Pragmatism
chapterSources.note: Truth is what it is good for us to believe: not relativism but a different criterion for when disciplined approximation counts as knowledge.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Most Objective We Can Be (Which Is, Admittedly, Not Very)

chapterSources.author: John Dewey
chapterSources.title: The Quest for Certainty
chapterSources.note: The philosophical disease is seeking absolute foundations; the cure is treating inquiry as an ongoing activity in the world rather than a transcendent achievement.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Most Objective We Can Be (Which Is, Admittedly, Not Very)

chapterSources.author: Hannah Arendt
chapterSources.title: The Human Condition
chapterSources.note: Natality, promising, and forgiving: the ethics of irreversible action in a plural world; every act sets off unpredictable chains and that is the risk we take.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Use the Blade, Build the World

chapterSources.author: Iris Murdoch
chapterSources.title: The Sovereignty of Good
chapterSources.note: The primary moral task is accurate perception. Use the blade means cutting through self-deception; build the world means attending to what is actually there.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Use the Blade, Build the World

chapterSources.author: Albert Camus
chapterSources.title: The Myth of Sisyphus
chapterSources.note: Revolt against the absurd: the act of world-making is its own meaning, not a means to meaning. One must imagine Sisyphus happy.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Use the Blade, Build the World

chapterSources.author: Ruth Chang
chapterSources.title: Incommensurability, Incomparability, and Practical Reason
chapterSources.note: Hard choices are constitutive: by committing, we create reasons and make ourselves. The absence of a determinate best option is an invitation to self-authorship.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Use the Blade, Build the World

chapterSources.author: Emmanuel Levinas
chapterSources.title: Ethics as First Philosophy
chapterSources.note: Infinite responsibility to the face of the Other precedes ontology and epistemology; the world being built is always with and for others.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Use the Blade, Build the World

chapterSources.author: Derek Parfit
chapterSources.title: Reasons and Persons
chapterSources.note: Future selves are distinct persons who deserve consideration. The small acts that accumulate across a life are owed to someone who is not quite you.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Use the Blade, Build the World

chapterSources.author: Simone de Beauvoir
chapterSources.title: The Ethics of Ambiguity
chapterSources.note: Freedom is not a private achievement. Use the blade well means using it toward a world where the blade is available to all.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Use the Blade, Build the World

chapterSources.author: Ernest Becker
chapterSources.title: The Denial of Death
chapterSources.note: The heroic project: we build worlds because we know we will die. Every act of world-making is simultaneously a refusal of meaninglessness and a wager against finitude.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Use the Blade, Build the World

chapterSources.author: Merleau-Ponty
chapterSources.title: Phenomenology of Perception
chapterSources.note: Rigorous first-person method: pure description steering between reductionism and intellectualism without appealing to either.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: On Attempting to Explain Everything (Again)

chapterSources.author: Thomas Nagel
chapterSources.title: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
chapterSources.note: Defends the irreducibility of the first-person viewpoint: factor it out and there is nothing left of the experience.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: On Attempting to Explain Everything (Again)

chapterSources.author: Kierkegaard
chapterSources.title: Concluding Unscientific Postscript
chapterSources.note: The title is deliberate: indirect communication from a situated, exploratory stance rather than a philosophical system.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: On Attempting to Explain Everything (Again)

chapterSources.author: William James
chapterSources.title: Essays in Radical Empiricism
chapterSources.note: Pre-conceptual pure experience as the one fundamental stuff; all claims revisable by their lived consequences.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: On Attempting to Explain Everything (Again)

chapterSources.author: Wittgenstein
chapterSources.title: Philosophical Investigations
chapterSources.note: Language-games embed meaning in lived practice; even the most intimate experience can only be marked through shared, revisable frameworks.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: On Attempting to Explain Everything (Again)

chapterSources.author: Dan Zahavi
chapterSources.title: Subjectivity and Selfhood
chapterSources.note: Contemporary synthesis of Husserl and Merleau-Ponty: pre-reflective self-awareness as the structural foundation of all experience.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: On Attempting to Explain Everything (Again)

chapterSources.author: Ernest Becker
chapterSources.title: The Denial of Death
chapterSources.note: Awareness of our own mortality is precisely what makes human wanting 'unnatural': we cannot live purely on instinct because we know we will die, and that knowledge forces us to construct meaning rather than merely respond.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: On Attempting to Explain Everything (Again)

chapterSources.author: Antonio Damasio
chapterSources.title: Descartes' Error
chapterSources.note: Damasio's somatic-marker hypothesis connects bodily signals with decision-making; it does not prove that all life has human-like feelings.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Before Thought, There Is Want

chapterSources.author: Spinoza
chapterSources.title: Ethics, Part III
chapterSources.note: A classic account of striving and desire as central to how a being persists and evaluates its world.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Before Thought, There Is Want

chapterSources.author: Varela, Thompson & Rosch
chapterSources.title: The Embodied Mind
chapterSources.note: An enactive account of cognition as something living bodies do in relation to their environments.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Before Thought, There Is Want

chapterSources.author: William James
chapterSources.title: A Pluralistic Universe
chapterSources.note: A defense of a world containing genuinely different perspectives and unfinished relations.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Will Creates Difference, Which Creates Problems

chapterSources.author: Gilbert Simondon
chapterSources.title: Individuation in Light of Notions of Form and Information
chapterSources.note: A demanding account of individuals as processes formed through tensions, rather than sealed objects.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Will Creates Difference, Which Creates Problems

chapterSources.author: W. Brian Arthur
chapterSources.title: Increasing Returns and Path Dependence in the Economy
chapterSources.note: A model of how small earlier differences can shape later options through feedback; its economic claims should not be treated as a theory of every identity.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Will Creates Difference, Which Creates Problems

chapterSources.author: Martin Buber
chapterSources.title: I and Thou
chapterSources.note: A philosophical account of meeting another person as a someone rather than treating them only as an object of use.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Love, Growth, and Meaning (Which Are, It Turns Out, Related)

chapterSources.author: Iris Murdoch
chapterSources.title: The Sovereignty of Good
chapterSources.note: A case for loving attention as a moral practice: learning to see another person less through the lens of our own wishes.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Love, Growth, and Meaning (Which Are, It Turns Out, Related)

chapterSources.author: Susan Wolf
chapterSources.title: Meaning in Life and Why It Matters
chapterSources.note: A useful challenge to the idea that meaning is only personal desire; she connects meaningfulness with active engagement in worthwhile projects.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Love, Growth, and Meaning (Which Are, It Turns Out, Related)

chapterSources.author: Harry Frankfurt
chapterSources.title: The Importance of What We Care About
chapterSources.note: An account of how caring helps organize a life over time, while leaving open which objects of care deserve endorsement.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Love, Growth, and Meaning (Which Are, It Turns Out, Related)

chapterSources.author: Thomas Nagel
chapterSources.title: The View from Nowhere
chapterSources.note: A clear account of objectivity as an ideal that grows by stepping back from a particular point of view without escaping all points of view.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: From Subjectivity to Something That Will Have to Do

chapterSources.author: Hannah Arendt
chapterSources.title: The Human Condition
chapterSources.note: Plurality and a common world: many distinct people can be concerned with the same durable things.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: From Subjectivity to Something That Will Have to Do

chapterSources.author: Miranda Fricker
chapterSources.title: Epistemic Injustice
chapterSources.note: A necessary complication: shared knowledge can be distorted when a person's testimony is discounted or when a group lacks the concepts needed to describe its experience.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: From Subjectivity to Something That Will Have to Do

chapterSources.author: Maturana & Varela
chapterSources.title: Autopoiesis and Cognition
chapterSources.note: A living system maintains itself through ongoing interaction with its surroundings; its boundary is an achievement, not a wall.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The First Blade: The Catastrophic Invention of Edges

chapterSources.author: Jakob von Uexküll
chapterSources.title: A Foray into the Worlds of Animals and Humans
chapterSources.note: Different creatures inhabit different usable worlds because their senses and tasks select different features.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The First Blade: The Catastrophic Invention of Edges

chapterSources.author: Polly Matzinger
chapterSources.title: The Danger Model: A Renewed Sense of Self
chapterSources.note: Immune response cannot be reduced to a simple self-versus-foreign rule; damage and context also matter.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The First Blade: The Catastrophic Invention of Edges

chapterSources.author: C. S. Peirce
chapterSources.title: The Fixation of Belief
chapterSources.note: Inquiry earns its keep by exposing beliefs to evidence that can resist them.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Second Blade: Map and Territory

chapterSources.author: Andy Clark
chapterSources.title: Surfing Uncertainty
chapterSources.note: An influential account of perception as prediction constrained by sensory input, not a passive copy of the world.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Second Blade: Map and Territory

chapterSources.author: Douglas Hofstadter
chapterSources.title: I Am a Strange Loop
chapterSources.note: A provocative account of selves as self-referential patterns rather than hidden inner objects.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Second Blade: Map and Territory

chapterSources.author: Kent Berridge
chapterSources.title: Dissecting Components of Reward: Liking, Wanting, and Learning
chapterSources.note: Wanting, enjoyment, and learning can come apart; a strong urge is not proof that something will satisfy.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Third Blade: Good, Bad, and the Trouble with Both

chapterSources.author: Martha Nussbaum
chapterSources.title: Upheavals of Thought
chapterSources.note: An account of emotions as appraisals of what matters, open to criticism and education.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Third Blade: Good, Bad, and the Trouble with Both

chapterSources.author: Philippa Foot
chapterSources.title: Natural Goodness
chapterSources.note: A challenge to the idea that moral goodness follows straightforwardly from what helps an organism flourish.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Third Blade: Good, Bad, and the Trouble with Both

chapterSources.author: Eleanor Rosch
chapterSources.title: Principles of Categorization
chapterSources.note: Categories often have prototypes and fuzzy edges rather than fixed properties shared by every member.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Foundational Dualities

chapterSources.author: Mary Douglas
chapterSources.title: Purity and Danger
chapterSources.note: A classic account of how social order is maintained through classifications, including what is treated as out of place.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Foundational Dualities

chapterSources.author: Iris Marion Young
chapterSources.title: Justice and the Politics of Difference
chapterSources.note: A case for taking group difference seriously without treating groups as internally uniform or naturally opposed.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Foundational Dualities

chapterSources.author: Ian Hacking
chapterSources.title: Making Up People
chapterSources.note: Classifications of people can alter how people understand and act, changing the category in return.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Thingification

chapterSources.author: John Searle
chapterSources.title: The Construction of Social Reality
chapterSources.note: An account of how shared rules create institutional facts such as money and offices.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Thingification

chapterSources.author: James C. Scott
chapterSources.title: Seeing Like a State
chapterSources.note: Large institutions gain coordination through simplified categories, often at a human cost.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Thingification

chapterSources.author: Claude Shannon
chapterSources.title: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
chapterSources.note: A foundational account of signals and transmission; it deliberately does not settle what a message means or whether it is true.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Information / Physical Duality

chapterSources.author: Terrence Deacon
chapterSources.title: Incomplete Nature
chapterSources.note: An ambitious attempt to explain how organisms and signs carry aboutness without treating meaning as magic.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Information / Physical Duality

chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Information / Physical Duality

chapterSources.author: Donald T. Campbell
chapterSources.title: Assessing the Impact of Planned Social Change

chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Cost of the Blade

chapterSources.author: Ian Hacking
chapterSources.title: The Social Construction of What?

chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Cost of the Blade

chapterSources.author: Simone de Beauvoir
chapterSources.title: The Second Sex

chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Cost of the Blade

chapterSources.author: Kurt Gödel
chapterSources.title: On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems

chapterSources.chapterTitle: Knowledge, or the Shape of the Information Realm

chapterSources.author: Torkel Franzén
chapterSources.title: Gödel's Theorem: An Incomplete Guide to Its Use and Abuse
chapterSources.note: A lucid account of what incompleteness does and does not imply outside mathematical logic.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Knowledge, or the Shape of the Information Realm

chapterSources.author: Helen Longino
chapterSources.title: Science as Social Knowledge
chapterSources.note: Objectivity depends partly on criticism, shared standards, and whether varied perspectives can challenge a claim.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Knowledge, or the Shape of the Information Realm

chapterSources.author: Chris Argyris
chapterSources.title: Double Loop Learning in Organizations
chapterSources.note: Distinguishes correcting an action from reconsidering the governing goal or assumption.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Three Ways to Meet a Problem

chapterSources.author: Henry L. Roediger III and Jeffrey D. Karpicke
chapterSources.title: Test-Enhanced Learning
chapterSources.note: Experiments showing that retrieving studied material can improve later retention compared with repeated study under the tested conditions.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Learning: Measure, Model, Manipulate

chapterSources.author: James Woodward
chapterSources.title: Making Things Happen
chapterSources.note: A careful interventionist account of causal explanation and the assumptions interventions require.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Learning: Measure, Model, Manipulate

chapterSources.author: Peter M. Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran
chapterSources.title: Implementation Intentions and Goal Achievement

chapterSources.author: James C. Scott
chapterSources.title: Seeing Like a State

chapterSources.chapterTitle: Creating: Map, Move, Make

chapterSources.author: Martin Buber
chapterSources.title: I and Thou

chapterSources.chapterTitle: Becoming: Marvel, Meander, Manifest

chapterSources.title: Meaning in Life and Why It Matters

chapterSources.chapterTitle: Becoming: Marvel, Meander, Manifest

chapterSources.title: The Reflective Practitioner

chapterSources.chapterTitle: Choosing a Mode

chapterSources.author: W. Ross Ashby
chapterSources.title: An Introduction to Cybernetics

chapterSources.chapterTitle: Loops That Learn—and Loops That Don't

chapterSources.author: John Dewey
chapterSources.title: Experience and Education

chapterSources.chapterTitle: Loops That Learn—and Loops That Don't

chapterSources.author: Elinor Ostrom
chapterSources.title: Beyond Markets and States: Polycentric Governance of Complex Economic Systems

chapterSources.author: Geoffrey C. Bowker and Susan Leigh Star
chapterSources.title: Sorting Things Out

chapterSources.chapterTitle: What Knowledge Needs to Stay Alive

chapterSources.author: Elinor Ostrom
chapterSources.title: Governing the Commons
chapterSources.note: Case-based analysis of institutions people have used to govern shared resources, emphasizing fit to local conditions.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Changing a World We Share

chapterSources.author: Amartya Sen
chapterSources.title: The Idea of Justice

chapterSources.chapterTitle: Changing a World We Share

chapterSources.title: Information Technology and Economic Change: The Impact of the Printing Press

chapterSources.chapterTitle: Changing a World We Share

chapterSources.author: Barry M. Leiner and others
chapterSources.title: A Brief History of the Internet

chapterSources.chapterTitle: Changing a World We Share

chapterSources.author: Richard Lewontin
chapterSources.title: The Units of Selection
chapterSources.note: A classic statement of variation, differential fitness, and heredity as conditions for evolution by natural selection.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: How Far Does the Pattern Travel?

chapterSources.author: Francisco Varela, Evan Thompson, and Eleanor Rosch
chapterSources.title: The Embodied Mind

chapterSources.chapterTitle: How Far Does the Pattern Travel?

chapterSources.title: Enchiridion

chapterSources.title: MN 10: Mindfulness Meditation

chapterSources.chapterTitle: Practices Before Patterns

chapterSources.author: Pierre Hadot
chapterSources.title: Philosophy as a Way of Life

chapterSources.title: Science as Social Knowledge

chapterSources.chapterTitle: The Most Objective We Can Be

chapterSources.title: The Human Condition

chapterSources.chapterTitle: Use the Blade, Build the World

chapterSources.author: Simone de Beauvoir
chapterSources.title: The Ethics of Ambiguity
chapterSources.note: Freedom is shared and unfinished; a useful challenge to treating a good life as a private optimization project.

chapterSources.author: Iris Murdoch
chapterSources.title: The Sovereignty of Good
chapterSources.note: A case for moral attention: seeing another person more accurately can be an ethical act before it becomes a plan.
chapterSources.chapterTitle: Use the Blade, Build the World

chapterSources.author: Carlo Rovelli
chapterSources.title: The Order of Time

chapterSources.title: Essays in Radical Empiricism

chapterSources.title: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
chapterSources.note: A reminder that a description from outside does not exhaust what experience is like from inside.
